title: Peace
lead: Hebrew shalom is wholeness and well-being, not only the end of war: health, safety, right relations with God and neighbor. The prophets promise a Prince of Peace; the New Testament announces peace with God through Christ, peace between Jew and Gentile, and peace as the mark of a church. Early Christian writers, above all 1 Clement, made peace and harmony the cure for a divided church.

sections.b: Shalom covers a person's health, a city's safety, a covenant kept and a life whole before God. The priests' blessing ends with it: "May the LORD lift up his face toward you and grant you peace" (Numbers 6:26). It comes with justice: "What righteousness makes will be peace" (Isaiah 32:17), and "righteousness and peace have kissed" (Psalm 85:10). Even exiles are told, "Seek the peace of the city I sent you to as exiles, and pray for it to the LORD" (Jeremiah 29:7). The coming king is the "Prince of Peace" (Isaiah 9:6), and the false prophets are those who cry peace when there is none (Jeremiah 6:14).
sections.refs: Numbers 6:24-26; Isaiah 32:17; Psalm 85:10; Jeremiah 29:7; Isaiah 9:6; Jeremiah 6:14; Isaiah 53:5

sections.h: Peace with God and peace with one another
sections.b: The angels sing of "peace among people he delights in" (Luke 2:14), and Jesus says, "I am leaving you peace. My own peace is what I give you" (John 14:27). Paul's gospel is peace with God: "We have been justified by faith. So we have peace with God, through our Lord Jesus Christ" (Romans 5:1). Christ "is himself our peace", who broke down the wall between Jew and Gentile (Ephesians 2:14). So peace becomes the church's task: "Let the peace of Christ be the umpire in your hearts" (Colossians 3:15); "God is not a God of disorder but of peace" (1 Corinthians 14:33); "Blessed are the peacemakers" (Matthew 5:9).
